newsitem.title: UK: Budget,summer holidays prompt UK housing lull-RICS.
newsitem.headline: Budget,summer holidays prompt UK housing lull-RICS.

text.p: Britain's burgeoning housing market paused for breath in July as the holiday season got underway and people pondered the twin effects of the budget and a series of interest rate rises.

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors said the net balance of chartered surveyors across the country reporting price increases over the three months to the end of July fell to 54 percent, from 56 in June. In July last year, that balance, which measures the difference between the percentage who reported price rises and the percentage who said prices fell, was just 32 percent.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown cut mortgage interest relief to 10 percent from 15 in his July 2 budget and raised stamp duty on houses costing more than 250,000 pounds.
Base rates have been ratcheted up in four quarter-point moves, taking them to seven percent, since Labour snatched power on May 1.
The RICS said the regional divide of recent months, which has seen house prices in London and the South East rocket while the rest of the country has lagged, is fading.
"Our survey shows that the housing market recovery can no longer be seen as a purely southern phenomenon," said Ian Perry, RICS housing spokesman.

"The wide regional imbalances of the past 12 months have started to fade as buyers in the South are frustrated by the lack of properties and the high prices in the South have fuelled price rises in other parts of the country." Supply shortages continue to pose a problem with buyers in Greater London and the South East being forced to delay their move in many cases.
Prices are forecast to rise by almost 10 percent this year, slowing to six percent in 1998 as more properties come onto the market.
"We expect the market to slow down next year...as more people put their homes up for sale," Perry said.
